section.heading: 3.9. Related Rates
section.paragraph: If we are pumping air into a balloon, both the volume and the radius of the balloon are increasing and their rates of increase are related to each other. But it is much easier to measure directly the rate of increase of the volume than the rate of increase of the radius.

In a related rates problem the idea is to compute the rate of change of one quantity in terms of the rate of change of another quantity (which may be more easily measured). The procedure is to find an equation that relates the two quantities and then use the Chain Rule to differentiate both sides with respect to time.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Air is being pumped into a spherical balloon so that its volume increases at a rate of $$100{{cm}^{3} \slash s}$$ . How fast is the radius of the balloon increasing when the diameter is $$50$$ cm?

According to the Principles of Problem Solving discussed following Chapter 1, the first step is to understand the problem. This includes reading the problem carefully, identifying the given and the unknown, and introducing suitable notation.
Solution We start by identifying two things:
the given information:

list.item: the rate of increase of the volume of air is $$100{{cm}^{3} \slash s}$$

example.paragraph: and the unknown:

list.item: the rate of increase of the radius when the diameter is $$50$$ cm

example.paragraph: In order to express these quantities mathematically, we introduce some suggestive notation:

list.item: Let $$V$$ be the volume of the balloon and let $$r$$ be its radius.

example.paragraph: The key thing to remember is that rates of change are derivatives. In this problem, the volume and the radius are both functions of the time $$t$$ . The rate of increase of the volume with respect to time is the derivative $$dV \slash dt$$ , and the rate of increase of the radius is $$dr \slash dt$$ . We can therefore restate the given and the unknown as follows:
$$\begin{array}{ll} {\mathit{Given}:} & { \frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}} = 100{{cm}^{3} \slash s}} \\ {\mathit{Unknown}:} & { \frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}} {when}r = 25{cm}} \end{array}$$
The second stage of problem solving is to think of a plan for connecting the given and the unknown.
In order to connect $$dV \slash dt$$ and $$dr \slash dt$$ , we first relate $$V$$ and $$r$$ by a formula—in this case, the formula for the volume of a sphere:
In order to use the given information, we differentiate each side of this equation with respect to $$t$$ . To differentiate the right side, we need to use the Chain Rule:
$$\frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{dV}{\mathit{dr}}\frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}} = 4\pi r^{2}\frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}}$$
Now we solve for the unknown quantity:
$$\frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{4\pi r^{2}}\frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}}$$
If we put $$r = 25$$ and $$dV \slash dt = 100$$ in this equation, we obtain
$$\frac{\mathit{dr}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{4\pi(25)^{2}}100 = \frac{1}{25\pi}$$
The radius of the balloon is increasing at the rate of $$1 \slash \left( {25\pi} \right) \approx 0.0127{{cm} \slash s}$$ when the diameter is $$50{cm}$$ .
Notice that, although $${dV} \slash \mathit{dt}$$ is constant, $$\mathit{dr} \slash \mathit{dt}$$ is not constant.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: A ladder $$10$$ ft long rests against a vertical wall. If the bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall at a rate of $$4{{ft} \slash s}$$ , how fast is the top of the ladder sliding down the wall when the bottom of the ladder is $$6$$ ft from the wall?

Solution We first draw a diagram and label it as in Figure 1. Let $$x$$ feet be the distance from the bottom of the ladder to the wall and $$y$$ feet the distance from the top of the ladder to the ground. Note that $$x$$ and $$y$$ are both functions of $$t$$ (time, measured in seconds).

image.alt: Details An illustration shows a vertical wall standing perpendicular to the horizontal ground. A ladder of length 10 feet is leaning against the wall. The horizontal distance from the bottom of the wall to the base of the ladder is labeled x. The vertical distance from the ground to the top of the ladder is labeled y.

example.paragraph: We are given that $$\mathit{dx} \slash dt = 4{{ft} \slash s}$$ and we are asked to find $$\mathit{dy} \slash dt$$ when $$x = 6$$ ft (see Figure 2). In this problem, the relationship between $$x$$ and $$y$$ is given by the Pythagorean Theorem:
Differentiating each side with respect to $$t$$ using the Chain Rule, we have
$$2x\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} + 2y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} = 0$$
Solving this equation for the desired rate, we obtain
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{x}{y}\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}$$

image.alt: Details An illustration shows a vertical wall standing perpendicular to the horizontal ground. A ladder is leaning against the wall. The horizontal distance from the bottom of the wall to the base of the ladder is labeled x. The vertical distance from the ground to the top of the ladder is labeled y. Below the ground, there is a rightward arrow, and the equation below reads, d x/d t = 4. Beside the wall, there is a downward arrow, and the equation reads, d y/d t = question mark.

example.paragraph: When $$x = 6$$ , the Pythagorean Theorem gives $$y = 8$$ and so, substituting these values and $$\mathit{dx} \slash dt = 4$$ , we have
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{6}{8}(4) = - 3{ft} \slash s$$

The fact that $$\mathit{dy} \slash dt$$ is negative means that the distance from the top of the ladder to the ground is decreasing at a rate of $$3{{ft} \slash s}$$ . In other words, the top of the ladder is sliding down the wall at a rate of $$3{{ft} \slash s}$$ .

note.title: Problem Solving Strategy
note.heading: Problem Solving Strategy
note.paragraph: Look back: What have we learned from Examples 1 and 2 that will help us solve future problems?
It is useful to recall some of the problem-solving principles and adapt them to related rates in light of our experience in Examples 1 and 2:

list.item: Introduce notation. Assign symbols to all quantities that are functions of time.
Express the given information and the required rate in terms of derivatives.
Write an equation that relates the various quantities of the problem. If necessary, use the geometry of the situation to eliminate one of the variables by substitution (see Example 3).
Use the Chain Rule to differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $$t$$ .
Substitute the given information into the resulting equation and solve for the unknown rate.

note.paragraph: See also Principles of Problem Solving following Chapter 1.

section.paragraph: Warning A common error is to substitute the given numerical information (for quantities that vary with time) too early. This should be done only after the differentiation. (Step 7 follows Step 6.) For instance, in Example 1 we dealt with general values of $$r$$ until we finally substituted $$r = 25$$ at the last step. (If we had put $$r = 25$$ earlier, we would have gotten $$dV \slash dt = 0$$ , which is clearly wrong.)
The following examples further illustrate this strategy.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: A water tank has the shape of an inverted circular cone with base radius $$2$$ m and height $$4$$ m. If water is being pumped into the tank at a rate of $$2{m^{3} \slash \min}$$ , find the rate at which the water level is rising when the water is $$3$$ m deep.

Solution We first sketch the cone and label it as in Figure 3. Let $$V$$ , $$r$$ , and $$h$$ be the volume of the water, the radius of the surface, and the height of the water at time $$t$$ , where $$t$$ is measured in minutes.

image.alt: Details An illustration shows a three-dimensional inverted cone of radius 2 units and height 4 units. This cone is partially filled with water. The water level rises to a height of h units. The base of the water level has radius r units.

example.paragraph: We are given that $$dV \slash dt = 2{m^{3} \slash \min}$$ and we are asked to find $$dh \slash dt$$ when $$h$$ is $$3$$ m. The quantities $$V$$ and $$h$$ are related by the equation
but it is very useful to express $$V$$ as a function of $$h$$ alone. In order to eliminate $$r$$ , we use the similar triangles in Figure 3 to write
and the expression for $$V$$ becomes
$$V = \frac{1}{3}\pi\left( \frac{h}{2} \right)^{2}h = \frac{\pi}{12}h^{3}$$
Now we can differentiate each side with respect to $$t$$ :
$$\frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{\pi}{4}h^{2}\frac{\mathit{dh}}{\mathit{dt}}$$
so
$$\frac{\mathit{dh}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{4}{\pi h^{2}}\frac{dV}{\mathit{dt}}$$
Substituting $$h = 3$$ m and $$dV \slash dt = 2{m^{3} \slash \min}$$ , we have
$$\frac{\mathit{dh}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{4}{\pi(3)^{2}} \cdot 2 = \frac{8}{9\pi}$$
The water level is rising at a rate of $$8 \slash \left( {9\pi} \right) \approx 0.28{m \slash \min}$$ .

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Car A is traveling west at $$50{{mi} \slash h}$$ and car B is traveling north at $$60{{mi} \slash h}$$ . Both are headed for the intersection of the two roads. At what rate are the cars approaching each other when car A is $$0.3$$ mi and car B is $$0.4$$ mi from the intersection?

Solution We draw Figure 4, where $$C$$ is the intersection of the roads. At a given time $$t$$ , let $$x$$ be the distance from car $$A$$ to $$C$$ , let $$y$$ be the distance from car $$B$$ to $$C$$ , and let $$z$$ be the distance between the cars, where $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ are measured in miles.

image.alt: Details A figure shows a horizontal line and a vertical line intersecting at point C. Point A is marked on the horizontal line x units to the right of point C. Point B is marked on the vertical line y units below point C, where x > y. A horizontal line segment connects points A and C with an arrow flowing leftward from point A to point C. A vertical line segment connects points B and C with an arrow flowing upward from point B to point C. The direct distance connecting point A and point B is labeled z, thus forming a right triangle A C B.

example.paragraph: We are given that $$\mathit{dx} \slash dt = - 50{{mi} \slash h}$$ and $$\mathit{dy} \slash dt = - 60{{mi} \slash h}$$ . (The derivatives are negative because $$x$$ and $$y$$ are decreasing.) We are asked to find $$dz \slash dt$$ . The equation that relates $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ is given by the Pythagorean Theorem:
Differentiating each side with respect to $$t$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{rll} {2z\frac{dz}{\mathit{dt}}} & = & {2x\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} + 2y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}}} \\ \frac{dz}{\mathit{dt}} & = & {\frac{1}{z}\left( {x\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} + y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}}} \right)} \end{array}$$
When $$x = 0.3$$ mi and $$y = 0.4$$ mi, the Pythagorean Theorem gives $$z = 0.5$$ mi, so

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{dz}{\mathit{dt}} = {\frac{1}{0.5}\left\lbrack {0.3\left( {- 50} \right) + 0.4\left( {- 60} \right)} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dz}{\mathit{dt}}} = {- 78{mi} \slash h}} \end{array}$$
The cars are approaching each other at a rate of $$78{mi} \slash h$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: A man walks along a straight path at a speed of $$4{{ft} \slash s}$$ . A spotlight is located on the ground $$20$$ ft from the path and is kept focused on the man. At what rate is the spotlight rotating when the man is $$15$$ ft from the point on the path closest to the light?

Solution We draw Figure 5 and let $$x$$ be the distance from the man to the point on the path closest to the spotlight. We let $$\theta$$ be the angle between the beam of the light and the perpendicular to the path.

image.alt: Details An illustration shows a spotlight focusing on a man who walks along a horizontal straight path. The spotlight is at a vertical distance of 20 units from the horizontal path below it. A perpendicular of length 20 units is drawn from the spotlight to the horizontal path. The man is at a horizontal distance of x units from the perpendicular. Thus we have a right triangle with base x units, and the vertical side of length 20 units. A diagonal line segment connecting the spotlight and the man acts as the hypotenuse. The angle at the spotlight, between the hypotenuse and the perpendicular, is labeled theta.

example.paragraph: We are given that $$\mathit{dx} \slash dt = 4{{ft} \slash s}$$ and are asked to find $$d\theta \slash dt$$ when $$x = 15$$ . The equation that relates $$x$$ and $$\theta$$ can be written from Figure 5:
$${\frac{x}{20} = \tan\theta} {x = 20\tan\theta}$$
Differentiating each side with respect to $$t$$ , we get
$$\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} = 20\sec^{2}\theta\frac{d\theta}{\mathit{dt}}$$
so

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{d\theta}{\mathit{dt}} = {\frac{1}{20}\cos^{2}\theta\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d\theta}{\mathit{dt}}} = {\frac{1}{20}\cos^{2}\theta(4) = \frac{1}{5}\cos^{2}\theta}} \end{array}$$
When $$x = 15$$ , the length of the beam is $$25$$ , so $$\cos\theta = \frac{20}{25} = \frac{4}{5}$$ and
$$\frac{d\theta}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{5}\left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^{2} = \frac{16}{125} = 0.128$$
The spotlight is rotating at a rate of $$0.128{{rad} \slash s}$$ .
$$0.128\frac{rad}{s} \times \frac{1{rotation}}{2\pi{rad}} \times \frac{60s}{1\min} \approx 1.22{rotations per min}$$
